## What this is for

`v_forecast_divergence` (sql/ad4_16_nws.sql) measures how far apart two
forecast models are about the same day, and probability_engine.py widens
sigma by that spread. With only ONE model in `weather_forecasts` the spread
is always 0 and the multiplier is always 1.0 - i.e. the whole mechanism is
dormant.

This workflow is the second model. It writes NWS's own hourly gridpoint
forecast as `model='nws'`, beside the Open-Meteo rows the Actions job
already writes. That is what switches divergence on.

The multiplier has a FLOOR of 1.0, so this can only ever make AD4 LESS
confident than its measured historical skill says - never more. A second
opinion is allowed to add doubt, not certainty.

## How a daily max is derived, and what is deliberately dropped

NWS publishes an HOURLY forecast, not a daily maximum. This takes the max
across each LOCAL calendar day - `startTime` comes back with the gridpoint's
own UTC offset, so the first 10 characters are the local date, no timezone
table needed.

A day is only written if the hourly series actually covers the PEAK WINDOW
(local 12:00-18:00 by default). This matters more than it sounds:

  * the series starts at the current hour, so running this at 20:00 gives a
    "today" whose hours all sit after the peak
  * the far end of the range (~156h) stops mid-day

In both cases the max of what is present is BELOW the real forecast max. A
too-low number here does not just lose a day - it manufactures fake spread
against Open-Meteo, and fake spread widens sigma for no reason. So partial
days are skipped rather than written.

`run_at` is NWS's own `updateTime` (the issuance), not the time this ran, so
re-running between issuances updates rows in place instead of piling up.
